title: Counting Milestones at GRUSK – Andy Karr
content:
Set amongst ancient rock formations and a million acres of National Forest, the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob has become a fixture of the mid-Atlantic gravel circuit over its decade of existence. Andy Karr brought his gravel bike, a camera, and two dozen of his closest friends up to the Seneca Rocks and Spruce Knob area of West Virginia to celebrate a series of big life milestones at this year’s GRUSK.

That the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob fell on my fortieth birthday was serendipitous. GRUSK has been a popular event for me and my Great Eskape teammates since 2017, and we’ve routinely made a weekend of it. We usually set up camp for our teammates and other friends for Friday and Saturday nights at the nearby Seneca Shadows campground. A weekend of camping, riding bikes, and hanging out around a campfire sounded like a great way to ring in decade number four.

Forty being widely held as a milestone birthday, a fair number of friends, family, and coworkers have asked me if I “feel old” turning forty this year.

Old? Wanna know what’s old?

The quartzite and limestone that now make up the distinctive geological features on Spruce Knob and the nearby Seneca Rocks in West Virginia are formed from sediments deposited on a seabed 450-600 million years ago. The spines of Seneca Rocks are sedimentary layers upended and turned 90 degrees on their side by the collision of a chain of volcanos (now the Blue Ridge) with the North American Plate over 200 million years ago. Nothing sets the anxieties of middle age into a proper deep-time context like holding a birthday party in a setting shaped by tectonic and erosional forces over hundreds of millions of years.

For the last ten of those years, the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob has been bringing adventurous cyclists together for a weekend of gravel riding, camping, and companionship in the middle of the Spruce Knob-Seneca Rocks National Recreation Area and its many crags and hollows (pronounced “hollers,” around here). In addition to hosting West Virginia’s tallest point, the Spruce Knob area is crisscrossed by streams and rivers, plentiful blankets of rhododendron and laurel flowers, nearly a million acres of Monongahela National Forest, and by hundreds of miles of gravel roads and doubletrack that make for endless possibilities for gravel riding routes.

Travis, GRUSK’s founder and (along with his wife Rachel) principal organizer, has been riding bikes in the Spruce Knob area since well before the term “gravel bike” came into wide use. Though getting to fishing spots was the primary reason for his earliest cycling adventures in the area, a precursor to GRUSK came about at the invite-only New Year’s Eve Ride Up Spruce Knob in 2010.

Evolution of GRUSK

The idea for GRUSK itself was born on a birthday ride. Travis rode to the top of Spruce from Seneca Rocks with a good friend for their birthday, during which they schemed up a gravel event on Spruce. Shortly thereafter, another promoter failed to launch a proposed 3-day stage race on Spruce Knob. Travis offered to help pitch in, and before he knew it, he was planning the first GRUSK.

This year was the 10th running of GRUSK. Over the last decade, it has evolved and changed as the “gravel scene” has changed around it. GRUSK was run for years as the Gravel Race Up Spruce Knob, but the infusion of hypercompetitive, more road-race-like attitudes and the worry of racing on open roads with traffic and blind corners weighed heavily on Travis and Rachel. Eventually GRUSK evolved towards a granfondo-style event with competitive segments, to eventually the non-competitive fondo style it is now.

The shift in approach not only meant a safer event, but also a shift in resources away from prize purses and towards improving the experience of all riders. Travis tells me he fully expected the event to die once the competitive element was removed, but the year following the transition to non-competitive actually had a boost in ridership over prior years. I think I speak for the vast majority of GRUSK riders in saying that it’s one of the most exceptionally well-run aid station and rider logistical experiences of any event I have done.

The route itself has shifted over the last decade. As the bikepacking format gained popularity, longer and longer routes have been added to the trio of single-day distances. The route design has also been altered to improve rider safety by avoiding some of the sketchier road descents and high-traffic stretches. In earlier years the route summited Spruce Knob near the end of the day – however, both careless drivers in rented jeeps and thunderstorms are much more common on Spruce in the afternoon, so the summit was moved to earlier in the day.

I’ve ridden GRUSK five or six of the ten times it’s been run. I know substantial changes have been made over the years, but they’ve not impacted the character of the route enough for me to really notice. It’s a beautiful route. It’s challenging without being grueling. I’ve done the 50-mile version, the now-defunct 75-mile version, and the 89-mile version – always scaled to my level of fitness at the time – so no year stands out as particularly hard or easy. As a bike ride, GRUSK has been consistent and dependable, bordering on ritualistic. It’s a fixture in the yearly ride/race schedule for the team and me. But GRUSK is, and has always been, more than just a bike ride. It’s been a good excuse to get the increasingly geographically dispersed and busy-lifed gang together, see old friends, and throw down for a long weekend in the woods.

The Core of GRUSK

It’s all possible thanks to Travis, Rachel, and their small army of volunteers and local fire departments. Between the local bike shops that have supported the event with prizes, neutral aid, and even dry places for the bikepackers to rest, the local residents who wave and cheer us on throughout the ride, and the support of local leadership in working with GRUSK and its riders to fuel a growing outdoor tourism economy, GRUSK has been a catalyst of community building for a decade. I asked what running this event for the last decade has meant to Travis.

“Over the years, GRUSK has meant doing something bigger than yourself, building a community and showing the beauty of West Virginia to the cycling world beyond mountain biking. GRUSK has meant hard work, lots of long nights, and the usual blood, sweat, and tears event management brings. GRUSK has also meant thousands of smiles, dirty finish line hugs, campfire stories, and so many kind words from riders about the event. The results have been incredibly rewarding. I’ve strengthened friendships, forged new ones, and worked through differences in opinions to bring a quality event to every participant.”

Reflections at This Year’s GRUSK

GRUSK’s tenth year running was the perfect catalyst to draw together some communities of my own. Also celebrating tenth anniversaries this year are the bicycle club I co-founded with some of my best friends and DC’s Coffee Outside Ride series, which I’ve been attending since its inception in 2016. GRUSK 2026 falling on my 40th birthday this year meant that the group campout at Seneca Shadows was more than just a team affair – it brought together friends I’ve made through Coffee Outside, Great Eskape teammates, a ragtag group of other bike friends, Sarah, our dog Indie, and friends who’d be unlikely to sign up to ride up the side of a mountain.

Most, but not all, of us who camped together rode GRUSK. It was the impetus for all of this, after all. But the weekend was a lot more than a bike ride. We gathered around campfires, jumped into chilly swimming holes, cracked out our favorite camp stove recipes, marveled at fireflies, and joked and laughed deep into the night.

Gathering at GRUSK, and the decision to celebrate some big milestones there this year, laid bare some important reflections about the last decade. All the team rides, campfires, mugs of coffee, and front porch hangs offered more than a good time and memories. They connected people. I cherish the friendships I have made over the last ten years of this very bike-centric lifestyle. I am also immensely proud of the friendships these folks have made with each other at everything from events like GRUSK to semi-weekly coffee rides.

This community has really tied the last decade together, and I’m feeling upbeat about how it will grow, strengthen, and evolve.

As for GRUSK, rumors are that this may have been the last running of the event. I asked Travis after the event what the future holds for him, Rachel, and GRUSK. He said that the future was ambiguous.

“This may not be the last year of GRUSK, but it is the last year Rachel and I, along with our core group of friends, manage the day-to-day operations. It takes an immense amount of time and work to put on GRUSK every year, and the timing feels right to pass the torch over to someone with more time and energy to take the reins. We hope we can find the right person/company who will commit to keeping the spirit of GRUSK alive… We’re planning a small group tour to Italy in spring for the Strade Bianche and another small group tour to go watch and ride the routes for the first week of the Tour de France. There could be another gravel event in the future or maybe a gravel camp; we have lots of ideas, but who knows? We’re just going where our wheels lead us.”
